⚔ Tactical Command — Field Manual

Controls

  • LMB select unit · drag for box-select · Shift adds to selection · double-click selects all of a type
  • Orders, the Close Combat way. RMB on one of your men selects his section and opens its order menu: Move Z · Move Fast X · Sneak C · Fire V · Smoke B · Defend N · Ambush M — click one, or press its letter while the menu is open. An order the section cannot carry out is greyed, with the reason on it (an immobilised tank cannot move; nobody without smoke can lay it). A move then wants a left-click on the map and leaves a dot in its colour — blue Move, yellow Sneak, purple Move Fast — which you can drag to send them somewhere else; hold Shift to click a route of legs and let go of it to send them. Fire brings up the targeting circle on a line from every man: the line is light green where he can see, dark green through foliage or smoke and red where something is in the way (orange and brown for mortars, which can fire blind), with the range to the obstruction written on it; the circle is white over nobody and, over a man you have spotted, green, yellow, red or black for the chance the order kills him; the number beside it is the range, green within effective range, yellow beyond it, black out of reach. Defend and Ambush stop the men, put them into the nearest cover and turn them to face a blue or green arc — drag the arc to turn them; an ambush holds its fire until the enemy is inside 30 m. How they go matters, as it did in Close Combat: on a Move they stop to fight anything they see on the way and then go on to where they were going; on Move Fast they run, see little, tire quickly and never stop to shoot — though a man in their way gets the bayonet; on Sneak they crawl, see the most, are the hardest to spot and never open fire first. A Move or a Move Fast ends in Defend, a Sneak in Ambush. Shells coming in put men flat, but an order is not cancelled by it — they go on once the fire has passed, and a section told to Defend or lie in Ambush goes back to it. With men selected, a right-click on the ground or on an enemy opens their menu too, so a man too small to hit is never in the way — and an aimed order always waits for your click, wherever the menu was opened (hold Shift to click a route of legs). A click anywhere off the menu, or Esc, throws it away; a right-click throws away an order that is waiting for its click. More orders ▸ at the foot of the menu holds everything else (assault, routes, hold, prone, dig, face, the shell natures, squads, transport, engineers), and it is where the old order bar can be switched back on · Ctrl/Cmd+A select everyone
  • Clicking on a section. A rifleman is about eight pixels wide at the playing camera, so the click no longer has to land on him: anything within a generous radius of a man selects his whole section, with the nearest to the cursor winning and your own troops taking priority over the enemy's on the left button (and on the right, whichever of the two the pointer is nearer — yours on a tie). Dragging a box takes whole sections too, and catches a man whose body is inside the box even when his boots are not. Alt still means "just this soldier". Double-click takes every one of that type on screen.
  • Your section fights with you in direct control. Take over one man with V and the rest of his section conforms to him instead of standing where you left them. They form a wedge in his lee and match his pace when he moves; they go firm in an arc facing his sightline when he stops; and the moment he is in contact they split the way they are trained to — the men who can see the threat go down and put fire on it, the rest work round its flank, and somebody puts smoke up if he is being cut to pieces. The split is a national habit: an American squad puts a heavy base of fire down and envelops wide, a German one keeps the assault group small. Nobody walks in front of the man you are aiming with.
  • Waypoints on every move order. Shift queues a leg for any way of moving, not just a plain march, and each leg remembers the mode it was given in — so one set of orders can read "walk to the hedge, crawl across the gap, run the last fifty metres, then assault the barn". Arm F Fast, N Sneak or M Assault and hold shift while you click to keep laying legs in that mode. The order lines draw each leg in its own colour. Works for infantry, guns and armour alike, and for squads given the Close Combat orders.
  • Ctrl+Click attack the ground: one deliberate volley onto the spot — guns and mortars shell it, the rest fire at it
  • WASD/arrows pan · Q/E rotate · middle-mouse drag orbits · scroll zooms
  • Space pause · Tab toggle editor · X stop · H hold ground · T scatter · 1–9 formations (re-forms instantly; 7 Vee, 8/9 echelon) · 0 cycles spacing (Tight/Open/Dispersed — distance between men is the answer to artillery). A mixed selection layers itself: armour leads, riflemen follow in its lee, support weapons trail
  • K then click a spot to lob smoke (billowing screens that cut line of sight) · Shift+V toggle fog of war · O toggle order lines · I toggle the LOS overlay · Shift+T toggle tactical counters · V take direct control
  • Vision is a CONE, not a circle — every unit sees a wedge in the way it faces (tanks narrower, snipers narrowest); up close it's 360°. Idle, holding, defending and ambushing troops scan left and right. Units turn toward gunfire/movement they sense, then acquire — so you can be flanked from outside a unit's gaze.
  • Face / watch (Z / ◑ Face, then click) — turn the selected units to watch a direction (a tank rotates its whole hull) and hold that arc. Set your defensive arcs before the enemy arrives.
  • Tactical counters (Shift+T / ⊞ Counters): from above, a battalion is brown dots in a green field. This puts a NATO counter over every section you can see — the branch symbol (crossed diagonals infantry, a dot for a machine gun, an oval for armour, an inverted V for mortars), its name, how many men are left, a strength bar and what it is doing right now. Your men always; the enemy's only where somebody of yours can actually see them. The counters fade out as you come down to ground level, because by then you can see the men.
  • LOS overlay (I / ◎ LOS): paints each selected unit's view cone — green where it can both see and shoot, blue where it can only see. Crests, walls and hedges cut it off.
  • Direct control — ride ANY unit (V / ⌾ Direct with one unit selected). You take the man's place:
    • On foot — W forward, S back, A/D step left and right (all relative to where you look), Shift sprint, C crouch, Z prone, Q/E lean left and right round cover. In anything you DRIVE, A and D turn the machine instead of stepping. LMB fires — a semi-automatic (the Garand, the carbine, a pistol) as fast as you pull the trigger, a bolt action once the bolt has been worked, an automatic at its real cyclic rate while held. RMB (or wheel-up) brings the weapon to the eye on its own sights: an open notch with the post in it, or an aperture drawn as the eye sees one, a soft ring round the front post — iron sights barely magnify, and a sniper's scope is its real power (2.5× to 4×). Every weapon has its magazine, clip or belt: R reloads (a Kar98k a clip or a round at a time, a Garand only when its clip has pinged out — or after throwing a part-spent one out), and an empty one starts its reload when you let go of the trigger. B is the fire selector (single shot or automatic; the BAR's slow and fast rates), 1/2 the rifle and the pistol (machine gunners, paratroopers, snipers and officers carry one), X fixes the bayonet and F strikes with it — or with the butt. G pulls the pin: hold it to cook the grenade and let go to throw — you carry the two or four your army issued, they reach thirty to forty metres, and a time fuse that outlasts the flight leaves it lying fizzing where it lands. K pops smoke where you're looking, Y digs in. Under fire the view flinches and drops — a man being shot at does not sightsee, and that is most of what suppression is.
    • In a tank — H works the hatch. Head out you can see: full field of view, and the crew spots nearly thirty per cent further. Closed down you are looking through vision blocks — the field of view narrows, the edges close in, the crew see a third less, and you are safe. Almost every commander in Normandy fought head out and a great many of them were killed doing it; a rifle round or a mortar splinter that cannot touch the tank can very easily touch him, and if it does the hatch slams and the gun goes quiet. 1/2/3 call AP/HE/WP to the loader, 4 hands the choice back to him, 5 calls for the tungsten round where the gun has one (below) and B steps to the next nature aboard; the rack strip above the loading gauge shows the nature you called (outlined), the round actually going up the spout (lit) and how many of each are left (an empty rack is struck through). An anti-tank gun's crew answer to the same keys.
    • In a tank — W/S drive, A/D traverse the hull, mouse lays the turret, LMB fires the main gun and RMB works the coaxial MG.
    • Behind a gun — the crew traverse the piece with the mouse; L limbers/unlimbers it. Mortar and howitzer crews fire indirect at whatever the sight is on.
    • Tab steps to the next unit without leaving first person · V/Esc hands the unit back to its own orders.
    Your own dispersion is real: the crosshair blooms when you move, when you're suppressed and on sustained fire, and tightens when you go prone or aim down the sights.
  • Order lines (selected units): on-ground move paths in Close Combat's colours — blue move / yellow sneak / purple fast — plus fire vectors — red direct / orange obstructed / yellow indirect
  • Squads (dual-layer command): select 2+ units and press J (or ⧉ Squad) to form a squad — each gets a coloured ground ring. Click any member to select the whole squad; Alt-click a member to command it alone while the rest hold their task. The squad leader (an officer if present) steadies the team's aim and recovers their suppression; being pinned spreads to squadmates. Squads move in their own formation (1–9). Shift+J splits units back out
  • Buildings: right-click a house/building with infantry selected and choose Enter building to occupy it — defenders gain hard cover and elevated sightlines from upper-floor windows. Dig them out with HE or flame. U leaves the building
  • Cover & foliage: stone/brick/concrete walls, trenches and earthworks give hard cover; woods (pine, oak, scrub) and hedges conceal you and let some bullets whip through the leaves
  • Transports: right-click a friendly halftrack/truck/APC with infantry selected and choose Board (or press Enter) to load them for fast, armoured transport (safe from small arms). ▢ Unload to debark. A heavy AT hit that brews the transport wipes most of the squad inside
  • Reinforcements (right-hand panel, under Call for fire) — one scrollable list of everything you can put on the field, at the three sizes an army is actually organised in. Packages at the top are delivered by a transport that drives in from the map edge. Then Sections & squads: a whole Rifle Squad, a Gruppe, a company HQ — the complete formation with the right men in the right proportions, arriving as a real squad with its own leader, cohesion, morale and roster line. Then Weapons teams — the machine-gun, mortar, anti-tank and reconnaissance detachments. Then Guns, armour & transport. Then every individual unit in the game, for when what you need is one bazooka man. Each row shows its strength (12×); your own army comes first in every band — worked out from the men actually on the field, so the Soviet list is on top at Prokhorovka — and everything else is marked with a ·. The filter box searches names, types and nationalities at once (try mortar, or soviet). Pick a row, click a drop zone, and the formation marches on from the nearest edge and forms up on it. It is all free. There is no cost, no reserve to run down and no cooldown to wait out — ask for a Tiger every thirty seconds if that is the battle you want. (The enemy commander still fights out of a finite reserve of his own, so there is still a battle at the end of it.)
  • Order bar (off by default — More orders ▸ Show the order bar brings it back along the bottom) — the Close Combat orders on the top row, every other order on the second, and the bar only shows what the current selection can actually perform: no Prone for a tank, no engineer charges without an engineer. The posture your men are already in is lit gold, and an order waiting for you to click a point on the map pulses, with the hint line under the bar telling you what it wants. Every button carries its hotkey.
  • Keys without the menu (the letters inside the menu are Close Combat's; these work any time a section is selected): F move fast · N sneak · G defend · R take cover · P prone · M assault · Z face/watch · Y dig in · L limber gun · B ambush · C hide · H hold · X stop · I LOS cone · V direct control (Shift+V fog of war)
  • Assault (M, then click an objective): the selection bounds forward by fire-and-movement — half the men go prone and suppress while the other half rush the next tranche, then they swap, all the way onto the objective. The classic way to cross open ground alive.
  • Engineers (buttons): Mine, Wire, Hedgehog, Demo — select an engineer, click the button, then click a spot.
  • Ctrl+Click area fire: pound a ground spot — ranged units keep suppressing it until their ammo runs dry.
  • The section is the unit of manoeuvre — the commander gives orders to squads, not to men, and each one carries out a single task as a squad: hold an objective all-round and dug in, base of fire in cover with a sightline onto the objective, bound forward under its own covering fire, assault the last thirty metres under smoke, counter-attack ground just lost, sit in reserve, or break contact when the odds are bad. The fire element inside a section is the men with its heavy weapons — the MG42 team, the BAR man — so a German section and an American one behave differently without a single special case: theirs is built round the gun and takes it forward with the assault, ours stays put and shoots. Watch the Order of Battle panel: every section tells you what it is doing.
  • The company plan — the commander does not simply react to contact: he makes a scheme of manoeuvre and holds to it. A support-by-fire position is chosen because it overlooks the objective and sits on the opposite side from the assault; a flank is chosen because the ground there is covered and unwatched and because it is the side they are not facing. Then it runs in phases — form up · win the firefight · work round · assault · consolidate — and it does not go until the firefight is won. Watch the Order of Battle: a section reading Working round (unseen) is sneaking to its assembly area, Formed up, waiting is lying up in it holding its fire, and Fire lifted is the base of fire walking its rounds off the objective as the riflemen go in.
  • Smoke, sneaking and grenades — a section about to cross ground that is swept asks for a screen on it first, and a mortar fires it if one can reach. The approach to a flank is made at a crawl, because the whole value of a flank is that it was not seen coming. And a grenade is thrown at a man you cannot shoot — dug in, in a building, behind a wall — and into the position in the last thirty metres of an assault.
  • National doctrine — one playbook, two dialects. US Army 1944 wants a heavy base of fire, a wide envelopment and the artillery on the objective before anybody stands up. The Wehrmacht attacks in smaller groups with shorter rushes, defends in depth on reverse slopes, digs in harder, and counter-attacks immediately when it loses a position — the Gegenstoß — which is the single thing you will notice most when you take something off it.
  • Enemy doctrine — the AI fights by WWII fire-and-manoeuvre rather than swarming: machine guns and mortars lay a base of suppressive fire while rifle groups only bound forward when the odds favour them — otherwise they take cover and hold. Pin their support weapons and their attack stalls. The commander fights for the objectives: it marches on the nearest flag it doesn't own, garrisons and digs in on the ones it holds, drops registered artillery on any flag you're raising, angles its assaults onto contested rings under smoke — and when it's behind on flags with the clock running out, it strips its reserves and throws everything at the objective.

Tactical systems

  • Objectives & the clock — named flags stand on the field: the village, the crossroads, the crest, the bridge. Every stock map has five to nine of them and they sit on the ground that is actually worth holding; a map that names none has them read off its own terrain (built-up ground, prepared positions, commanding height, road junctions, crossings, defiles). Stand inside a ring with no enemy present to raise your flag (more men raise it faster; both sides inside freezes it). The top-bar timer (10 / 15 / 20 / 30 min / unlimited) counts down: at zero, whoever holds more flags wins — level on flags, the stronger surviving force takes it. Hold every flag for 45 s and the battle ends immediately, timer or not. Wiping the enemy out still wins, as ever. The floating pill up top shows the countdown and each flag in its owner's colour. Author your own objectives in Edit → Map → Objectives & plans: plant as many flags as you like at any ring size (click removes, Shift+click resizes); a map with none has them read off its terrain.
  • Force tab (editor) — Squads stamps a whole section in one click, and it arrives as a real squad: its own leader, formation, cohesion, squad morale and the eight Close Combat orders, not a heap of men standing near each other. Pick the side, the formation and the stance it should be found in — Dug in puts them in their holes already, which is what a defender would have done with the time. Below it, off-map fire support: how many missions of each battery that side may call during the battle. Give the defender a couple of mortar missions and an attack across open ground becomes a very different problem. The minimap shows both armies while you are editing and reverts to what your side can actually see the moment you press Play.
  • Battle plans (attack routes) — in Edit → Map, draw a route of waypoints for either side and press Finish route. When the battle starts, the route takes command of the units of that team standing nearest its first marker and walks them leg by leg under AI. Draw them for the enemy to script attacks against you, or for your own troops to fight a plan hands-free. Your own routes show as a faint trace in battle; the enemy's stay hidden.
  • ⇶ Route order (in battle) — select any units (an officer's squad, a tank platoon, the whole line) and press ⇶ Route in the palette: each left-click lays a waypoint, double-click / Enter / right-click launches, Esc cancels. The group then attacks along the route carefully, as a unit: nobody runs ahead of the formation, stragglers are waited for at every leg, men who hit contact are supported — the rest close in and add fire instead of marching on — the pinned scrape in where they lie, smoke goes up when the fire gets heavy, and the final waypoint is fortified. If the group loses nearly half its strength it breaks off and retires to the previous waypoint under smoke, digging in there. Any direct order to a soldier (or X Stop / H Hold) takes him back out of the plan.
  • 🧠 Auto-command (your own AI) — with the top-bar 🧠 Auto lit, your idle units fight the battle on their own initiative. Line troops and armour move on un-owned flags, keep two standing on every flag you hold, and dig in on station; the support weapons — MGs, snipers, AT guns, mortars — displace on their own to overwatch ground pulled back from the nearest contested flag (guns limber for the road and drop back into battery on arrival; MG teams scrape in on their gun line). Artillery stays where you sited it. Your hand always wins — anything you've ordered, selected, garrisoned, entrenched or put on a route is never touched, and an ordered unit only rejoins the autopilot ~12 s after its last order.
  • Guns can be manhandled — a deployed AT gun or howitzer no longer needs limbering for every adjustment: give it a move order and the crew heaves the piece at a crawl (about half walking pace). Limber (L) for anything farther than the next hedgerow.
  • Tank ammunition (AP / HE / WP) — select a tank and the palette offers three natures, as the real loaders carried: ▸AP solid shot defeats armour but its burst is a furrow in the dirt — near-useless against men in the open; ✸HE bursts wide and murders infantry, guns and buildings but will not defeat tank plate; ☈WP white phosphorus throws an instant smoke screen and splashes burning phosphorus over everything under it — a terror round. It does not look like high explosive and it is not meant to: the shell cracks rather than detonates, throws sixty burning wedges out in flat arcs that go on burning white where they land, and builds a brilliant white wall you cannot see through. Men caught in it burn white and panic. It will not cook a tank's ammunition the way a flame gun's fuel does — it blinds the crew and makes them get out. Click the lit nature to hand the choice back to the crew, who load sensibly on their own (shot for armour, HE for men, the odd WP round at dug-in defenders). In first person the loader answers to 1 AP · 2 HE · 3 WP · 4 his own judgement (shot for armour in the sight, HE for anything else), and B cycles; every round comes out of its own rack, and the strip on the sight says which. The tungsten round (5, or Tungsten on the order bar): the guns that had one in 1944–45 carry a handful — British APDS for the 17- and 6-pounder (the 17-pounder's very fast and notoriously wide), American HVAP for the 76 mm, the 3-inch and the 90 mm, German Pzgr 40 and Soviet BR-354P. Much more penetration up close, much less on a steep slope (the plate sees the thin core, not the gun's bore) and very little behind the plate; the crews keep it for the tank their ordinary shot cannot open, and so does the loader on crew's choice. A Firefly's APDS will open a Panther's glacis out to about a kilometre, where its APCBC never could; a 76 mm's HVAP only inside about 150 m, which is what the US Army found at Isigny in August 1944. Ammunition is stowage, not a resource bar — and it is stowed by nature: a Sherman carries ninety rounds of 75 mm, and they are thirty-four of shot and fifty-six of HE, not ninety of whatever you need next. Spend the morning shelling a hedgerow and the counter-attack is met with what is left in the other rack; when the shot runs out the loader answers with HE and the commander lives with it. The split is what the vehicle was for: an M10 is seventy per cent shot, a Firefly nearly two thirds, a StuG and a Brummbär mostly high explosive, an IS-2 eight rounds of shot out of twenty-eight. The gunsight reads AP n · HE n. Machine guns are stowed the same way and there is more than one of them: a Sherman has a coax, a bow gun in the glacis that fires while the turret is traversed somewhere else, and a .50 on the roof; a Firefly has only the coax, because the bow gunner's seat was plated over for 17-pdr rounds — which is also why it carries four men and a Sherman five. An M10 and a Hellcat have no coaxial gun at all, and an SU-76, SU-100, Marder and Nashorn have none mounted anywhere. Hose a hedgerow for ten minutes and the coax runs dry — the readout in the gunsight is rounds · nature · MG · smoke, and an ammunition truck refills both racks.
  • Lethality & fire — rifles and machine guns miss more and kill more: dispersion is up, but a round that connects usually ends a man, and a blast that overkills leaves no body to bury. Knocked-out tanks sometimes cook off: the fire finds the racked shells — cracks and sparks as rounds pop, then the magazine goes up and shreds everything nearby. Ammo trucks and loaded rocket launchers go up guaranteed, and huge — park them well back. Flamethrowers no longer "explode": the gout lands as burning fuel, sets men alight (a burning man panics, screams and dies unless he reaches water), and terrifies everyone who watched it land. Flame against armour is about the source, not the flame: a flame gun's thickened fuel clings to the plate and goes in through the louvres — a Crocodile burst usually bails the crew and often lights the tank outright — but burning ground is not an anti-tank weapon. A tank driving through a burning field takes nothing from it; one that parks in a fire cooks slowly over minutes, and its crew get out long before the machine does. A grass fire never cooks off ammunition, and fire that spreads on its own never carries the flame gun's bite with it.
  • ☎ Call for fire — the guns you never see. Off-map artillery, heavy mortars and air support, bought in the campaign's requisition or handed out in the editor's Force tab. You do not deploy them and you cannot lose them; you buy the right to call them, a fixed number of times. Click a battery in the Call for fire panel, then click the target.
    The delay is the whole point. A mortar section answers in eighteen seconds; a 155 battalion takes over a minute; an air strike nearly two. A fire mission is a decision about where the enemy will be, not where he is — which is exactly the problem a real forward observer had, and why ground you expect to be fought over is worth registering early. A ring on the map shows where yours will land and how long you have to get clear of it. The enemy commander has the same batteries and calls them the same way, and it does not show you the ring.
  • What a shell actually does. Blast and fear fall off gently; fragments do not — they spread over a circle that grows with the square of the distance and lose velocity the whole way out. So a heavy shell has a small lethal core and a wide wounding-and-terrifying penumbra, and the bigger the shell the sharper that split. A single 155 round kills a standing man out to about 25 m whatever he does, wounds out to 40 m, and mostly rattles beyond that.
    Which is why you dig. Fragments fly flat, so getting below the plane of the burst beats anything you could hide behind: a man in a scraped hole is out of the spray almost entirely, a man lying down is most of the way there, and a man standing in the open is a full-height target. Dispersion is the other answer — twelve heavy shells on a bunched platoon kill everyone in it, and the same twelve on a dispersed one kill half. Mortars are the counter to the hole, because a bomb dropping almost vertically bursts inside the cone the hole leaves open. Men caught inside a heavy burst who live are shell-shocked: deaf, disoriented, unable to shoot or follow an order for the better part of a minute.
  • The men are simulated, not the counters. Every soldier carries five attributes rolled individually — Morale (willingness to fight on), Leadership (how much he steadies the men near him), Intelligence (how likely he is to panic or go berserk), Strength (how fast he tires, how badly a wound hurts) and Experience (which makes him better at almost everything). An eight-man section is not eight average men: it is a couple who will hold when nobody else does, a couple who will break early, and four in the middle — and you do not get to know which is which in advance.
  • The condition ladder. A man does not go from fighting to running; he goes down a ladder, and at every rung he does less shooting and more hiding. Watch the coloured pip over his helmet:
    ■ Suppressed — taking cover, but still firing back.
    ■ Pinned — spending more time hiding than firing.
    ■ Cowering — head down, fires occasionally, will not move at all.
    ■ Panicked — combat efficiency gone; he may come round if you get a leader to him.
    ■ Broken — has stopped obeying orders and is thinking about running.
    ■ Routed — gone. He cannot be recovered.
    ■ Stunned — an explosion has knocked him out for a few seconds.
    And upward: ■ Heroic, and ■ Berserk — a man who feels invulnerable, attacks without fear, and steadies everyone who watches him do it. It is the frightened man who is not thinking clearly who goes berserk, which is exactly as it should be.
  • Your men can refuse. This is the rule the whole game rests on. Order a section across ground a machine gun is laid on, in the open, with nothing suppressing it, and they will not go — they will get down or get into the nearest cover instead, and tell you why. Same for walking riflemen at armour in the open, and same for a squad that has already broken. A frontal charge is not a tactic you can execute; it is a thing your soldiers decline to do. Suppress the gun, or smoke the gap, and the same order is obeyed. (The old behaviour is available: it is the "soldiers always obey" flag.)
  • Suppression is what fire is FOR. Rounds that miss now do the work — anything passing within about twelve metres of a man puts his head down, whether it was aimed at him or not. That single fact is what makes covering fire exist: one machine gun has a section pinned inside ten seconds without hitting anybody, a rifle section takes twenty-odd, and a mortar concentration forces infantry to hit the dirt without exposing your own troops at all. Fire, then move, then swap — that is the whole of infantry tactics and it now works because it has to.
  • Fatigue. Rested → Winded (recovers with a short break) → Fatigued (completely blown — he stops where he is and cannot act). Move Fast is speed you borrow and pay back lying in a ditch, heavy weapons crews tire faster, and a strong man lasts longer. It is why Move and Sneak are the orders you actually give.
  • Being flanked is a mechanic, not a metaphor. Fire arriving from two bearings at once costs a man his nerve far faster than the same weight from one, halves what his cover is worth (a wall only stops one of them) and makes it harder for him to shoot back — because he has to choose which way to face. Getting round a flank is worth the walk.
  • Hands up. A section whose position is hopeless does not always die or run: it surrenders. All four of the things that actually produced that have to be true at once — it is shaken or worse, it is cut off with none of its own within supporting distance, the enemy is close enough to take it, and it has no way out: out of ammunition, or its leader is down, or it has lost over half its strength. Then it is a roll against the men's own steadiness, whoever is still giving orders, and how badly they are outnumbered on the spot — so good troops under a good NCO go into the bag last. They put their weapons down, stand for a moment, and are gone; nobody shoots a man with his hands up, and they are not casualties — they are prisoners, and they count against the side that lost them. Watching the section next to you give up costs you something; taking them is worth something. This is the reward for encirclement: cut a section off and it may fold without a shot, which is what a company commander on either side spent the war trying to arrange.
  • Morale events. Losing an officer shakes everyone inside his command radius, and the better he was the worse it is. So does watching your armour burn, and so does lying among too many dead. The other way: springing an ambush steadies a whole section, and infantry killing a tank is the largest morale event in the game — because in 1944 it was.
  • Armour arcs are a movement order. Under Move or Sneak a tank crew keeps the thick plate toward whatever is shooting at them — they will reverse the whole way rather than show you their side. Under Move Fast they turn to face the destination and run, which hands their flank to anything watching. A sneaking tank is at maximum watchfulness and minimum speed; a running one sees almost nothing. Firing on the move costs rate of fire. All of which feeds the armour model that was already there: the plate that gets hit is decided by how you told them to move.
  • Armour follows infantry. Both commanders now hold their tanks back at gun range behind the riflemen, and will not drive up to a building the infantry have not walked through — because a tank on its own cannot see the man in it until he is close enough to kill it. Send infantry to find the target; let the tank shoot it from where it is safe.
  • Nobody stands in the open. Men who stop moving look for something to get behind before anyone fires at them, and if there is nothing within a short dash they lie down. They get up when they have somewhere to be.
  • The men have moods. Every squad carries a temperament — Aggressive, Steady, Cautious or Shaken — worked out from what a real section would be reacting to: how many of them are left, whether the man who gives the orders is still alive, how long they have been under fire without being able to answer it, whether the fight in front of them is going their way, how good they were to begin with, and a slow drift that is nobody's fault. It changes what they will actually do: an aggressive section assaults at worse than even odds and bounds in long rushes, a cautious one wants a better hand and digs instead, a shaken one will not move for anything. This is why suppressing a squad is worth as much as killing men in it.
  • Nobody moves alone. When part of a squad is up and crossing ground under fire, the rest of it goes flat, stops shooting at whatever it fancied, and covers the specific ground its mates are crossing — then they swap. And everyone in a section shoots at whatever is hurting one of them, in preference to their own targets. Fire and movement at the fire-team level, running underneath the commander's plan.
  • Both sides fight the same doctrine. There is one playbook in this game and two commanders using it. The enemy always has one; you have one too the moment you light 🧠 Auto, and it fights your side exactly the way the German commander fights his — base of fire, flanking bounds, a reserve held back and committed, smoke on the assault, artillery on the concentration, and giving ground when the odds are bad. Your hand always wins: order a unit, or just select it, and it hands control straight back to you for a few seconds.
  • ⚑ Seven campaigns, across five theatres and six years. Normandy as First Army and the Westheer holding it; A Bridge Too Far — sixty miles of one road with a division sitting on each bridge; the Eastern Front from both sides, as the Red Army from the Citadel at Brest to the Tiergarten and as the Ostheer going the other way; Desert and Mountain, Tobruk to the Argenta Gap; and The Fall of France, where you have the better tanks and six weeks. Seventy-seven battles over ninety-six fields. What carries over is your battlegroup: platoons of named squads that fought the last battle and are carrying its casualties into this one. Each campaign saves separately, so you can have all seven running at once.
  • The economy is the campaign — and you can switch it off. Winning pays requisition and losing pays half; difficulty is a supply setting rather than a damage slider (on Recruit you are carried by the supply chain, on Elite you live on what you take, and a victory is worth most there). The armies are shaped by the same arithmetic: the Red Army starts a third weaker than the Ostheer and crosses over in 1944, France's allowance falls every battle while the Wehrmacht's rises. Or tick Unlimited requisition — on the operation picker, or on the briefing screen of a campaign already in progress — for 999999 points and buy anything you like, as much of it as you like, at no cost: no prices, no scarcity caps and no waiting for a type to become available. Switch it back off whenever you like and the campaign economy resumes from the battle's own allowance; what you already bought is yours. Nine platoons of King Tigers at Brest if that is the afternoon you want. The enemy still buys out of its own pool against its own caps, so there is still a battle at the end of it.
  • ⛏ Deployment. Campaign battles open with the half hour before H-hour. Inside the shaded ground your men go wherever you right-click, instantly — no walking, they were already there — and Dig In is immediate, because they have had all night. Set postures, watch arcs and ambushes now. The clock does not run and neither does the enemy. Enter or Begin battle starts it. On the defence this is most of the battle; on the attack it is the difference between a start line and a shambles.
  • Real engagement ranges — one world unit is 4 m, and the field is 1.35 km across, so weapons reach what they historically reached: a rifle section fights out to ~480 m, an MG42 beats a zone at ~800 m, tank guns kill at 800–1000 m, and the 8.8 cm Flak ranges the entire valley. Panzerfausts and bazookas go the other way — they are 100–170 m ambush weapons. Past a weapon's effective range dispersion climbs steeply, so trading fire at a kilometre wastes ammunition: closing to decisive range still wins fights. Armour-piercing shot also loses bite with distance; shaped-charge rockets don't.
  • How you stand changes how you shoot — firing on the move throws rounds away, a man in the prone or resting over a parapet is far steadier, and tripods and gun carriages steadier still. Suppression and wounds widen the group; an officer nearby tightens it.
  • Weather & sky — clear, overcast, fog, rain, storm and snow each get their own sky: cloud decks lit from the sun's own bearing (so the silver lining is always on the right side of the cloud), a second deck of low scud racing under it on the wind, haze, a sun in the right place for the shadows, and lightning in a storm. Weather is not just a look — it cuts spotting range, spoils aim and slows movement.
  • Weather that changes. Pick 🌦 Changeable and weather stops being a setting and becomes a process: fronts come over during the battle. The light goes first, then the wind gets up, then it starts to rain — a few spots building to a downpour — and twenty minutes later it eases off again. Nothing jump-cuts; visibility, accuracy, the going underfoot, the sky and the wind are all walked across the transition together, and the toast line tells you what a soldier would have said about it.
  • Fog lies in the ground. Mist is not a uniform grey lid any more — it collects in the hollows, read off the map's own heightmap, and the banks drift downwind while you watch. A sightline through a bank is lost past a certain depth of it, so there is fog you can move a company through unseen and ground you can see clean across, and which you have decides your plan. Mist is low: a tank commander with his head out of the cupola, or an observer up on the crest, sees over the top of it.
  • Time of day (top bar) — the clock runs at real speed by default; scrub it to any hour, or run it at ×60 / ×300 / ×1200 to watch the light change. The sun follows a genuine solar model for 49° N, so the season sets the length of the day: a summer evening still has sun at eight o'clock and takes over an hour to go down through the golden hour and twilight, while a winter afternoon is dark by half four. Fighting at night is the single biggest spotting penalty in the game — muzzle flashes and tracers become the only way to find anyone.
  • Guns sound like guns — every weapon is placed in the world, so shots attenuate, lose their crack and pan with distance, and arrive late at the speed of sound: a gun firing a kilometre away flashes first and reaches you a beat later. Rounds snap past your head, shells whistle in before they land, tank guns roll their report off the treeline, and you can hear the breech open and the round go home while your own gun reloads.
  • Tracers — roughly one round in five is a tracer, exactly as the belts were loaded. Colour follows the army: Allied red, German green, Soviet lime — the two colours everybody who was shot at describes. The streak is the speed: it is drawn at the distance the round actually covers in the thirtieth of a second the eye integrates, so a .30-06 draws a thirty-metre bar and a Thompson an eight-metre one, and the element gutters as it burns out. Tank rounds are pointed shot with a driving band and a burning tracer in the base, scratching a vapour trail across the sky.
  • Real ballistics — every round now leaves the barrel at its own muzzle velocity and flies the trajectory that follows from it. A Sherman's 75 leaves at 619 m/s and a Panther's at 935: the same calibre, half again the speed, and that difference is the whole Normandy tank problem. The launch angle is solved from d = v² sin 2θ / g and the arc is a true parabola, so a Panther's shot is a straight line at a kilometre, a Char B1's 220 m/s hull howitzer visibly lobs, a Panzerfaust arcs over at eighteen degrees (which is why it is a ditch weapon at a hundred metres and a Panzerschreck is not), and a mortar bomb is fourteen seconds in the air and two hundred metres up. Mortar fire is called onto ground, not onto men, for exactly that reason.
  • Night fighting & lights (L / ✦ Lights) — torches and headlights throw a real beam down your sightline. They also make you a beacon: a lit unit is spotted from 2.6× as far away. See, or be seen.
  • Real rates of fire, fired by the manual — the MG42 hammers at its true 1200 rounds a minute inside a burst, the .50 cal at 550, a Thompson at 700 — and they are fired the way their gunners were taught: the MG42 in bursts of five to seven, about 150 rounds a minute sustained and 250 against an assault; the Browning .30 at sixty a minute it can keep up for half an hour; a Bren a magazine a minute, four in the rapid. A Garand fires as fast as the trigger is pulled and a Kar98k as fast as a trained man works its bolt and aims, about fifteen a minute. Every weapon reloads — eight-round clips, five-round chargers, magazines, pans and belts, each with its own drill and time — and a man carries what his army issued: 136 rounds for a GI, 65 for a German rifleman, 60 for a Tommy with two Bren magazines for the gun. Out of rounds he draws his pistol if he has one, and the bayonet goes on; an assault that reaches a position still held goes into it.
  • Fog of war — enemies stay hidden until one of your units has a clear line of sight; contact lingers briefly after you lose sight. A unit firing gives away its position.
  • Smoke (K, then click) — units that carry smoke rounds lob one to the spot; it blooms into a cloud that lingers, screening the sightline through its core (not a hard wall). Screen an advance or blind an anti-tank gun — but you only carry a few.
  • Armour & penetration — tanks have front/side/rear/top plates; a shell's effective armour rises with the impact angle (T ÷ cos θ). Angle your hull, and flank theirs — a round that bounces off the glacis penetrates the side. AP rounds lose bite at range; HEAT rockets don't.
  • Subsystems & brew-ups — a penetration can knock out the tracks/engine (immobilised), jam the gun, or cook off the ammo — a catastrophic brew-up that pops the turret and leaves a burning wreck spewing smoke that blocks sight. Dig in and dig deep.
  • Dig In (Y) & Take Cover (R) — infantry and gun crews can dig a foxhole (very heavy cover, low profile) after a short channel, or dash to the nearest cover object and hold.
  • Combat engineers — lay hidden mines that gut a tank's belly, string wire and hedgehogs to channel the enemy, and blow obstacles or bunkers with demolition satchels.
  • Close assault — what a rifleman does about a tank. Until now, nothing: outside the four launcher teams every infantryman in the game was carrying an anti-personnel grenade and was completely helpless against armour, which removes the whole reason a tank needs infantry with it. Every army issued something for this and most of it was horrible. Let the tank come past, get to its flank or its back deck, and put the charge on the thin plate — these all go in on the ROOF, which is why a German magnetic charge kills a Tiger that a Sherman's 75 mm cannot scratch from the front.
    What each army carries is a real difference and not a balance knob. A German grenadier wires six stick-grenade heads round a seventh and throws the bundle onto the engine deck; SS and Fallschirmjäger get the Hafthohlladung, a 110 mm shaped charge on three magnets that you have to walk up and stick on. Soviet sections carry Molotovs, and their officers the RPG-43. The British get the No. 74 sticky bomb, which everyone issued one disliked. The Japanese get the Type 99 magnetic mine. American riflemen get nothing at all — they had the bazooka and no standard hand-placed charge, so an American player fights armour with the launcher or not at all. Engineers on every side carry demolition satchels.
    Most of these do not destroy a tank and were never going to. A bundled charge, a satchel or a petrol bomb does not penetrate anything: it breaks the running gear, shakes the crew senseless and sometimes puts them out of the vehicle altogether — and an immobilised tank in the middle of a close assault is usually a dead one shortly afterwards. Only the shaped charges go through. It is also spent: two bundles, one magnetic mine, one sticky bomb, and then the section is back to being helpless. And it takes nerve — a man who is cowering or panicking will not walk up to a running tank, which is exactly why close assault needed cover, surprise, or a tank that had already stopped.
  • Towed guns (L) — anti-tank guns, the Flak 88 and the 155mm howitzer limber up to move and unlimber to fire (with a setup delay). Their crews are exposed: shell or spray a gun position and the crew dies, leaving the piece abandoned — walk any infantry onto it to re-crew it.
  • New iron — Tiger, Panther, Pershing, Stuart & M8, Puma, 155mm artillery, flamethrower teams, trucks, and officers whose presence steadies the men around them.
  • Four armies, and no alliances — a field can hold up to four sides, and every one of them is at war with every other. A Frenchman shooting at a German is not helping the Americans; he is taking the bridge for himself. Place teams 3 and 4 in the editor's Units tab (leave them empty for an ordinary two-sided battle), and look under Four Ways in the map list for two fields built for it. Team 0 is nobody's: an abandoned gun whose crew is dead, which fights no one until a section walks onto it and takes it over.
  • Ten more battles — Arnhem Bridge and Hell's Highway (a ramp held with no anti-tank gun, and a single embanked road you cannot leave); Ortona and Monte Cassino (a town fought through the walls, and a mountain with no cover on it at all); Kasserine Pass; Peleliu — Bloody Nose Ridge; Prokhorovka; Noville (fog, and armour coming out of it); Hill 262 — the Mace, held from inside the pocket it was corking; and Remagen, where the bridge was still standing.
  • Squads at their real establishment — a US rifle squad is twelve men as T/O&E 7-17 had it, not nine; a Schützengruppe is nine built round its MG42; an armoured Panzergrenadier Gruppe and a Fallschirmjäger Gruppe are ten with two MG42s; a machine gun is a five- or six-man squad and not a man with a friend, because one man cannot feed an M1919 and live; a sniper has an observer; and the Soviet squad finally has the DP-28 that was its entire base of fire.
  • Five more armies — France 1940 and the Maquis (Somua S35, Char B1 bis, the 47 APX, the FM 24/29); Italy (M13/40, Semovente 75/18, the Cannone da 47/32, Bersaglieri); Japan (Chi-Ha and Shinhoto, the Type 92 “woodpecker”, the knee mortar every section carried, and lunge-mine tank hunters); and the missing halves of the Red Army (DP-28, PTRD anti-tank rifle, T-34/76, KV-1, sappers and snipers), the Wehrmacht (Sturmgewehr 44, Panzer III, Brummbär, the PaK 43) and the US Army (carbine, grease gun, M4(105), M3 Lee, Marines and the Zippo flame tank). New fields for all of them: Gembloux, Stonne, Bir Hakeim, Takrouna, Tarawa, Edson's Ridge, Khalkhin Gol and Rzhev.
  • The rest of the order of battle — the units that were actually in the hedgerows and were missing.
    US: paratroopers and Rangers, the 60mm company mortar, medics who put a casualty back on the roster instead of in the return, the M7 Priest, and the M4A3E2 Jumbo — the one Sherman a Panther has to work at, bought with every bit of the mobility that made a Sherman worth having.
    Britain & Canada, who had no representation at all: a rifle section is not an American one — the Bren is a magazine gun where the BAR is, so British sustained fire is worse and they leant correspondingly harder on the Vickers, the 3-inch mortar and the 25-pounder. Plus the PIAT (a spring-launched bomb from a hundred metres, hopeless odds, and it will open a Tiger), Commandos, the Churchill AVRE and the Sherman Crab.
    Germany: Fallschirmjäger and SS-Panzergrenadiere, who did the actual fighting at Carentan and Caen and are categorically better than a static-division Grenadier — and the Ostbataillon at the other end of the same scale, Soviet prisoners in German uniform holding the coast because nobody better could be spared: numerous, cheap, and they will not stand. Plus the Panzerschreck (the bazooka done properly), the MG34 on its tripod, the 2cm Flak 38, the leFH 18 and sIG 33, the Jagdpanzer IV/70, and the Goliath — a wire-guided demolition carrier the size of a footstool that is nothing at all until it arrives.
  • Suppression — near-misses and explosions pin infantry: Normal → Cautious → Suppressed (slower fire, prone) → Pinned (can't move, wild aim). Machine guns exist to pin, not just to kill.
  • Lethality & wounds — gunfire is deadly but inaccurate: a hit in the open maims, but troops in cover are far harder to hit and take a fraction of the damage. Men pass through Healthy → Wounded (they hobble and shake, aim worse) and a solid hit often only knocks them Unconscious — a bleeding-out casualty who is out of the fight but can be stabilised by a medic before he dies. A burst, shell or overkill kills outright. Cover is now the single biggest thing keeping your men alive.
  • Prone (P) — drop to the dirt: the best posture cover in the open and a low silhouette, and unlike Hide the men keep firing. Crawling is slow — use it to hold a firing line, not to travel.
  • Crew bail-out — a tank that is immobilised and then either badly hurt or its crew terrified may be abandoned: the crew scramble out as near-helpless riflemen and run, leaving an inert wreck. Track a tank, keep hammering it, and you may rout the crew without killing the vehicle.
  • Ammunition — the WW2 detachment carries finite rounds (a bazooka team only 8). When a magazine runs dry the unit stops firing — keep them supplied and don't waste area fire.
  • Cover — foxholes, sandbags, walls, woods and buildings shield infantry from fire; mud and grass help a little. Fight from cover, and dig in (Defend) where there is none.
  • Shelling a building — what a gun does to a house depends on what is in the shell, and the difference decides how a village is fought. Armour-piercing is a solid slug: it punches a neat hole and carries on into the room — lethal to whoever is behind the wall, and it leaves the house standing. High explosive bursts, and what it takes down is a function of the bursting charge: 75mm opens a hole in brick, 105mm takes the panel out, 150mm removes the front of the house. A round that breaks through goes off inside. Timber and thatch do not resist at all and they burn; two feet of Norman rubble wall shrugs 75mm off all day, which is the most consistent complaint in the reports out of the bocage; and a shaped charge — a Panzerfaust — drills a fist-sized hole in masonry and leaves the building up.
  • Terrain — surfaces differ: roads speed you up; forest and rubble slow you but grant cover and concealment; mud and swamp bog you down. Fight from woods and broken ground.
  • Weather (top bar) — fog and rain cut how far you can see and shoot straight; rain and snow mire movement. Close unseen in bad weather, or hold and let them come to you.
  • Fortifications — trenches, gun pits, gabions, log walls, barricades and bunkers all give strong cover to hold ground — and they're destructible, so shell them out. Place them in the editor (Tab).
  • Stances — Sneak is a low crawl: the men go flat on their bellies, move at about a quarter of walking pace, and are spotted at roughly a quarter of the distance an upright man is. They get most of the prone posture's cover while they do it. It is how you cross the last hundred metres in front of a gun, and it is far too slow for anything else. Hide goes to ground and holds fire completely; Ambush waits hidden and unloads at close range; Move Fast is quicker but upright, loud and can't shoot; Defend digs in to hold. Combine them: crawl a squad into a treeline, set Ambush, and wait.
  • Mortars — 81mm / 8cm teams lob HE over hills and buildings onto anything a teammate can see. Deadly to infantry in the open and to open-topped vehicles; keep them back and screened.

Units

  • US Rifleman — fast-firing M1 carbine and a pineapple grenade for clustered targets. Ctrl+click throws the grenade at a spot.
  • Grenadier — Kar98k hits harder from further out but fires slowly; carries a stick grenade.
  • Sherman Jumbo / Panzer IV / Firefly / StuG / Achilles — tanks & tank destroyers. The main gun shells enemy armour first while the coaxial MG hoses infantry on its own trigger. Firefly's 17-pdr hits hardest; StuG has no turret (the hull aims); Achilles is open-topped and hates high explosive. Bullets ping off, shells and AT rockets punch through, wrecks burn.
  • Churchill Crocodile — closes in and sprays a gout of flame that ignores armour and annihilates infantry.
  • 8.8cm Flak / 7.5cm PaK 40 — crew-served anti-tank guns. Deadly at long range and hard to shift, but nearly immobile — flank them.
  • Bazooka / Panzerfaust — anti-tank rocket teams. One good shot wrecks a tank; slow to reload and weak against infantry.
  • MG42 / .50 cal — heavy machine guns. The MG42 is a buzzsaw against infantry; the .50 cal is slower but chews light vehicles too.
  • M3 / Sd.Kfz. 251 halftracks — fast, lightly-armoured MG carriers. Small arms hurt them where they'd bounce off a tank.

Field Tips

  • Height advantage grants bonus damage; attacking uphill is penalised.
  • Mud slows movement to a crawl. Cliffs steeper than ~2 blocks can't be climbed.
  • Craters deep enough will flood with water. You can dig moats with the Lower tool.
  • Your units defend themselves when idle but hold position while executing a move order — a retreat is a retreat.
  • Edit mode pauses the fight; switch back to resume exactly where it left off.
